objectives: Describe what is actually changing in the amount of time people spend together.
Name the forces behind the change and weigh them against each other.
Tell loneliness apart from solitude and from isolation.
Explain why some things still need a shared room.
Plan a gathering that people will come to and stay for.
Keep a friendship alive across distance without exhausting yourself.
Build shared time into a calendar without wrecking your week.

sections.body:
The claim that people are spending less time together is true in a narrow, measurable way and false in an important one, and separating the two is the first thing to get right.

What is measurably true: the number of **unplanned encounters** has fallen. In most large cities, people sit in cars, work at desks in separate rooms, shop in aisles they walk through alone, and go home to a flat where nobody else is. The chance of running into someone you know, and of that turning into a coffee, is much lower than it was twenty years ago. Public space has been designed so that you can pass through it without meeting anyone.

What is still true: when people choose to meet, they meet properly. The dinners, the weddings, the Sunday afternoons and the football matches have not become shorter. If anything, some of them have become longer, because a scheduled evening of time is now a deliberate event rather than the leftover of a free day.

So the change is not that people like each other less. The change is that **shared time has become scheduled instead of ambient**. It used to be a by-product of living in the same place. Now it has to be booked, like a meeting, and it competes with everything else on the calendar.

That shift has consequences, and they run in two directions. It makes it harder to make a new friend by accident, which makes new adult friendships rare and slow. It also makes the friendships people keep tend to be stronger, because they survived several rounds of deliberate effort. The word for the total quantity of shared time in your life is **social capital**: the value you get from your relationships, and the thing that gets weaker when those relationships are not maintained.

This article is about how to work with that shift rather than against it: how to notice the change, how to understand what is lost and what is gained, and how to put shared time back on a calendar where it survives contact with a busy week.
examples: We do not meet less often on purpose, we just run into each other less.
The evening was not shorter, we just had to book it.
sections.heading: What is actually changing

sections.body:
Three forces pushed in the same direction. None of them is a decision anybody made, which is why nobody feels responsible for the result.

The first is **busy**. Work hours have spread into evenings and weekends, commute times have grown in the cities where housing is affordable, and care work for children and older parents takes hours that used to be free. The time is not spent on screens; it is spent on the obligations that make up a life. When the diary is full, meeting people is the thing that gets dropped, because a message costs nothing and a dinner costs three hours.

The second is **the screen**. A phone gives you the social contact of other people without the friction of meeting them, and friction is what makes meetings real. It also removes the accidental encounters that used to create friendships, because the walk to the shop is now a walk alone. This force is not about people choosing devices over friends; it is that the device is always in your pocket, so the threshold for reaching out is almost zero, and every small message you send raises the bar for the bigger one.

The third is **friction and cost**. Meeting in person now takes planning, transport, money and energy. Two people in the same city who cannot meet on a Tuesday evening will meet on a Saturday, and a Saturday meeting is a bigger commitment, so it happens less often. The costs are not only financial: leaving the house, finding a babysitter, and recovering an evening are all real prices, and they are paid in the currency people have least of, which is attention.

These forces reinforce each other. A busy person sends a message instead of proposing a dinner. The message is fine, and so no dinner is proposed, and so the friendship moves to the category of things that always happen next week.
examples: I am not avoiding you, my week is simply full until Friday.
The message is easier than the dinner, so the message wins.
sections.heading: The three forces behind the change

sections.body:
Shared time used to sit outside the diary. It happened in corridors, at bus stops, in the queue at the shop, in the hour before somebody's train. Now the diary is the organising principle of a life, and anything that is not on it is at risk.

The most visible change is the working day. Many workplaces now expect a reply within minutes, and the tool that delivers the message also delivers the expectation. Work no longer has an edge. It has a beginning, a long middle and no end, and it fills the gaps that used to belong to other people. When a colleague writes at eleven at night and gets an answer, the message has cost the sender nothing and the receiver an evening.

The second change is that **plans are now countable**. You can see, on a shared calendar, how much time you have and who has what. This is useful for scheduling a wedding and awkward for everything else, because the most valuable shared time is usually the unplanned kind: the coffee that turned into three hours, the walk that went the long way.

The third change is the **planned and unpaid work of keeping up**. Friendships now require maintenance activity: answering messages, remembering dates, arranging the visit, sending the photograph. It is invisible labour, and it competes with paid work for the same hours.

The consequence is that **scheduling replaces drifting**, and drifting was where most deep friendships were built. The remedy is not to throw out the calendar. It is to enter the important shared things into the calendar with the same seriousness as a meeting, so that they are defended rather than negotiated every week.
examples: I am offline after six, and I am saying it out loud before somebody gets hurt.
We put the dinner in the calendar in January, which is the only reason it happens.
sections.heading: How the calendar took over

sections.body:
These words are used loosely in conversation, and using them precisely is the first step to thinking clearly about the subject.

**Presence** means being physically there and paying attention, as distinct from being logged in. **Social capital** is the value a person draws from their relationships and the trust that makes cooperation easy. **Social capital** is measured by how quickly a network of people can do something together, which is why organisations keep investing in it.

**Loneliness** is the gap between the number of relationships you want and the number you have. It is a feeling, not a measurement, and it can happen inside a full room. **Solitude** is being alone by choice, and it is not a problem at all. **Isolation** is being cut off from people, and unlike solitude it is not a choice and it does not feel restful.

**Proximity** is physical closeness. **Propinquity** is the effect of being near each other often: people who share a building, a class or a commute become friends without trying. **Community** is a group of people who share something and expect something of each other. **Belonging** is the feeling of being inside such a group rather than beside it.

**Ritual** is a repeated act that carries meaning beyond its content: the Sunday call, the Friday drink, the meal after the exam. **Continuity** is the sense that a friendship has a past and will have a future, which is what makes people keep investing in it. **Attention** is the resource that being together consumes, and it is the one people are shortest of.

**Async** describes communication that does not happen at the same time, such as a message thread or a recorded message. It is convenient and it is not a substitute for presence. **Broadcast** describes sending the same information to many people at once, which reaches them without reaching anybody in particular.
examples: That was presence, not just attendance.
I wanted solitude, not isolation, and the difference matters.
sections.heading: The words for being together and apart

terms.example: He was there, but his presence was somewhere else.
terms.gloss: Being physically there and paying attention, as distinct from being logged in or present in name only.

terms.example: A full calendar and a lonely February are not contradictions.
terms.gloss: The gap between the number of relationships you want and the number you actually have. It is a feeling, and it can occur in a crowded room.

terms.example: Two hours of solitude on Sunday is what makes the week work.
terms.gloss: Being alone by choice, with no element of loss or distress. It is not the same as loneliness.

terms.example: Working from home every day turned into isolation by February.
terms.gloss: Being cut off from other people without choosing it, and without the comfort that solitude brings.

terms.example: Propinquity did the work: we sat near each other for a year and then had a group chat.
terms.gloss: The effect of being near each other often. People who share a building or a class become friends without trying.

terms.example: The ritual is the point. The restaurant does not matter.
terms.gloss: A repeated act that carries meaning beyond its content, such as a Friday call or a Sunday lunch.

terms.example: A good boss spends a lot of the budget on building social capital.
terms.gloss: The value a person draws from their relationships, and the trust that makes working together easier.

sections.body:
Some things cannot be done through a screen, and it is worth knowing which ones, because these are the shared activities that survive and grow.

**Conflict and difficult conversations.** Anything where the tone of a voice, a pause or a held eye matters. Disagreement resolved badly over text can take months to repair; the same disagreement in a room usually takes an hour.

**Teaching and learning anything physical.** A skill with a body: cooking, repairs, sport, instruments, language pronunciation. It is much faster to be corrected in person than to be corrected in a comment.

**Grief, illness and caregiving.** These are the times people most often need to be physically available, and the most common reason people give for calling somebody rather than texting.

**Celebration and ritual.** Birthdays, weddings, the end of an exam, the last day of a job. These need witnesses. A shared meal with people who came for you is not the same event as a video call with the same people.

**Boredom.** This is the one people forget. Shared time that is not productive, that produces nothing, is exactly what most lonely people are missing. It cannot be scheduled as efficiently, and that is why it keeps being cut.

The practical lesson is that the events worth protecting are not the efficient ones. They are the ones where nothing needs to be decided. If you put a short, low-stakes, no-agenda gathering in the calendar once a week, it does more for your social life than a month of organising.
examples: This one is better face to face, because we need to talk about the hard part.
Come with nothing to plan. That is the whole point of it.
sections.heading: What still needs a shared room

sections.body:
This is a procedure that works, and it is deliberately small. The failure mode is trying to fix your social life with a plan, and then dropping the plan in week two.

The order matters because the hardest step is the first one, and because each step makes the next one easier.
examples: Sunday from six to nine at the usual place. If you cannot make it, tell me now.
No agenda tonight, just the table and whoever turns up.
sections.heading: How to get one real evening back
steps: Pick one person and one recurring slot, such as Sunday evening, and decide it is non-negotiable.
Put it in the calendar as an appointment with a location, not as a note in a list of intentions.
Invite two or three people to a fixed thing you already do, rather than inventing a new plan.
Set a start and an end time out loud, so nobody has to guess how long it runs.
Leave one slot free each week with no plans at all, and defend it.
Send one message a week to a friend whose messages you have been meaning to answer.
After a month, ask the two people you saw most whether you have become harder to reach.

sections.body: Loneliness is not fixed by adding people to a calendar. It is fixed by relationships that have continuity, reciprocity and a shared history, and those take repetition to build. Watch for the signs that solitude has tipped over into isolation: you have had no unplanned conversation in days, you begin to dread the messages you used to enjoy, the thought of meeting people costs more energy than it gives back, and you have stopped telling people what you did at the weekend. If two or more of those are true for more than a couple of weeks, the answer is not more screen time and not a busier calendar. It is one recurring, in-person, low-stakes commitment with people who know you, and a conversation you have been postponing.
examples: I have not spoken to anyone in person for four days, and I am noticing.
Let us do something with no agenda and no end time.
sections.heading: When being alone becomes isolation

sections.body:
The same forces have reached organisations, and the responses are visible if you know what to look for.

The first is the **scheduled shared hour**. Companies and teams have started putting a fixed lunch, a weekly walk or a Friday afternoon slot in the diary. It sounds trivial, and it is the single most effective intervention, because it makes contact a default rather than a favour. Teams that do it report a larger improvement in how information travels than teams that install collaboration software.

The second is **fewer, larger meetings**. Since remote work spread, the meeting count went up before it went down. The current practice is to keep meetings that need a room, cut the ones that only need information, and protect the time that the meetings were eating.

The third is the **third place**. Cafes, libraries, parks, community centres and shared workspaces exist so that people can be near each other without having to be with each other. This is the modern version of the street and the office lobby, and the reason some towns have started converting unused municipal buildings into them.

The fourth is **deliberate ritual**. Clubs, choirs, walking groups, sport leagues and volunteering organisations all do the same thing: they turn a loose interest into a fixed recurring event. From the outside this looks like a hobby. From the inside it is the cheapest and most reliable way to build social capital that has ever been found, because the attendance does not depend on anybody feeling motivated that evening.

The common thread is that all four make contact **predictable and scheduled**. That is the answer to the problem the calendar created.
examples: We have a lunch hour together on Wednesdays, and it is on the calendar.
The walking group is really just a way of making people see each other every week.
sections.heading: What workplaces and communities are doing about it

sections.body:
Before you plan anything, it helps to see the obstacles clearly, because each one has a different answer.

**Cost.** Two coffees and a taxi is not a big number, but it is a number, and it falls hardest on people with the least disposable income, which means the people with the most need for shared time are the ones who skip it. Cheaper formats matter: a walk, a square, a home, a free museum, a video call with the lights on.

**Distance.** Two people in different cities face a different problem from two people in the same city. Distance turns a meeting into an event, and events happen rarely. The countermeasure is to have two kinds of contact and not to confuse them: a cheap, frequent one, and an expensive, rare one. The frequent one keeps the friendship alive; the rare one keeps it real. People who skip the frequent one because it is not special end up doing nothing at all.

**Planning.** Shared time needs one person to do the work of proposing, and that person is usually the one with the least energy. This is why so many invitations fade: each person is waiting for the other to organise. The fix is to rotate the role, and to make the proposal smaller than you think it needs to be. "Coffee on Thursday, three o'clock, the place near the station" gets accepted. "We should really catch up sometime" does not.

**Appetite.** Some people want more shared time and some want less, and the negotiation is awkward because asking for more can sound needy and asking for less can sound cold. A direct sentence works better than a hint: "I would like to see you once a month, and I am happy with fortnightly if that is easier for you."
examples: Coffee on Thursday at three, the place near the station. Say yes or suggest another day.
Let us keep the weekly call small and book the proper dinner once a quarter.
sections.heading: The friction of meeting: cost, distance and planning

sections.body:
The useful conclusion is not that we should all get together more. It is that shared time has to be planned the way everything else in a busy life is planned, and that the plan has to be defended.

Start with the smallest thing that works. One recurring slot, with one or two people, in a place you can reach. Repeat it until it is boring, because boring is what makes a habit survive a bad week. Then add people slowly.

Second, keep **one shared thing** with the people closest to you. A meal on a fixed day, a call on a fixed morning, a sport on a fixed evening. The content matters less than the recurrence: a ritual that is unchanged for two years will hold a friendship together through a move, a job change and a bad year.

Third, do not confuse being together with being busy together. Shared time that is entirely scheduled, structured and productive is work with friends attached. The parts that people remember later are the unstructured parts: the walk after, the conversation in the car, the hour where nothing was decided.

Fourth, accept that the number of people you can do this with is small. Almost everybody has three or four relationships that could survive a year of very little contact, and a wide circle of people who are pleasant company but no obligation. The mistake is trying to maintain the second group at the same standard as the first. It is impossible, and the attempt is what makes people feel they are failing at friendship.

Fifth, be the person who makes the first move, and be easy to say yes to. The people who keep friendships alive are usually not the most popular ones; they are the ones who turn up.
examples: The same table, the same day, and nothing to plan.
You will not see everyone. That is not a failure, that is the shape of it.
sections.heading: How to be together on purpose

item.summary: People meet each other less than they did twenty years ago, and the reason is not that they stopped liking each other. After reading this you can explain the forces behind it, tell loneliness apart from solitude, plan shared time that people actually attend, and keep a friendship alive across distance and full calendars.
item.title: Why People Are Spending Less Time Together
